transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-09 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~82 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex (AE, Redwood), Samir (SE, Redwood), Jordan (Solutions, Redwood), Priya Nair (Infra Lead, Aeon), Tom Alvarez (ML Eng, Aeon), Susan Park (Head of Platform, Aeon)

Summary (auto):
Quick technical deep dive to validate options for reducing tail latency (p95/p99) for an internal real-time inference path. Focus: streaming vs batch, KV cache behaviour on their VPC topology, network hops through Transit Gateway/NAT, and quantization trade-offs. Intend to run a staging baseline and share artifacts.

Topics:
- p95/p99 targets (100ms/250ms goal)
- streaming chunk sizes vs non-streaming batching windows
- KV cache hotspot behavior and prefix caching
- multi-hop VPC egress and Transit Gateway impact
- quantization (int8 / q4) effects on throughput and tail variance

Action items (as captured above).

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: ok, thanks all for joining, uh we're gonna focus ideally on the p95/p99 stuff for the real time inference path. we got about an hour and change so we'll try to be practical.
[00:18] Priya: yep thanks. to set context, our production SLO is 100ms p95 and 250ms p99 for the human-facing assistant. today our observed p95 is around 140ms and p99 spikes to 420ms during bursts.
[00:32] Samir: got it. and quick question, is that measured from the app ingress or after your api gateway? like end-to-end or just inference node?
[00:44] Priya: it's end-to-end, app -> alb -> api gateway -> our service -> redwood endpoint. the redwood leg is around 40-60ms median, but tail seems worse.
[00:58] Tom: just to add, we see tail correlates with multi-segment requests where the model KV cache misses and we fall back to a cold kv load.
[01:12] Jordan: when you say "kv" do you mean Redwood's prefix cache / kv cache or your upstream KVS?
[01:20] Tom: the Redwood KV cache (we call it kv chache in our notes) — the hot key distribution is skewed, some prompts hit the same prefix and thrash the cache.
[01:35] Samir: that maps to what we often see — hotkeys + network concurrency creates stalls. two things we look at: (1) reduce network hops and (2) change batching/streaming behavior so hot prefixes are prefetched.
[01:48] Priya: can you expand on streaming vs non-streaming impact? we originally chose streaming to begin emitting partial tokens to UI, but we're thinking batching might be cheaper and maybe less tail-y?
[02:02] Samir: yeah, streaming often means more RPCs and smaller RPC payloads. you get lower median latency because you can start sending tokens earlier, but worst-case p99 can suffer due to extra network round trips if you have multi-hop NAT/transit path. batching (or micro-batching windows of 10-20ms) reduces per-token overhead and helps kernel-level throughput, but increases tail for small requests if you wait a batch window. it's a trade.
[02:29] Alex: holland note — also depends on the runtime's continuous batching. Redwood's serving runtime does continuous batching which tries to batch without adding a full window, but in certain setups (like cold KV cache and large model kv cache eviction) you still see tail spikes.
[02:45] Tom: about the network hop, Priya said we traverse a Transit Gateway and go out through a NAT in another AZ to reach Redwood Dedicated. that seems like two extra hops compared to direct peering.
[02:58] Priya: yes, peering wasn't available for our account; currently this is via shared transit and we have restricted egress.
[03:06] Samir: that can add 20-80ms variance depending on path and under load. if you can provide a staging VPC diagram we can point to exact hotspots — e.g. NAT queueing, ENI saturation.
[03:20] Susan: we can share that, but it's internal. we'll post to the secure link.
[03:28] Alex: great. Jordan, want to talk about profiling?
[03:33] Jordan: sure. what we recommend is a two-stage profiling: (A) generate a p95/p99 histogram for the end-to-end call and break down by service hop (client, nginx, app, redwood) and (B) run a focused redwood runtime trace that shows batching decisions, kv cache hit/miss, and kernel times. Samir, you had a profiler script?
[03:50] Samir: yeah I'll share a lightweight script that runs a sequence of 10k requests with mixed prefix distributions and outputs per-request latencies and a parsed p95/p99. it also annotates requests that triggered KV cache loads vs hits. it's a bit of a brittle infer profiler but should be useful.
[04:06] Tom: perfect. question — how does quantization affect tail? our model is a 7B-ish variant and we're evaluating int8 vs q4_0 quant configs.
[04:18] Samir: quantization reduces compute time and memory pressure but can increase variance slightly if kernels fall back or if quantization requires different kernel paths. int8 often has lower median and p95, but if the runtime has to decode/convert on CPU for certain layers, p99 can spike. q4_0 is usually stable on the GPU kernel path.
[04:36] Priya: is there a known interaction between quantized KV cache size and evictions?
[04:43] Jordan: yes, quantized KV caches are smaller per token, so you can retain more context, which reduces cold miss frequency. however if the KV cache implementation uses a shared pool and your hotkeys dominate, you still get eviction storms. tuning the cache shard size and pinning hot prefixes helps.
[05:02] [05:02] Tom: hmm, we saw a pattern where a long multi-turn early message causes a large kv footprint and triggers evictions for later short requests — which hurts p99.
[05:15] Samir: that's classic. options: prefix trimming, partial kv persists, or per-customer dedicated KV pool (reserved capacity).
[05:26] Priya: reserved capacity sounds good but we'd like to understand the cost tradeoff. Alex, can you send a pricing comparison for Dedicated vs Private plus notes on vpc peering options?
[05:36] Alex: yep, I'll send a snapshot.
[05:40] [05:40] Jordan: small note — we also recommend testing both streaming chunk sizes and micro-batching. e.g., streaming with 128-token chunk and aggressive prefix caching vs non-streaming with a 10ms micro-batch window. run both with the profiler and compare p95/p99 and token cost.
[05:58] Tom: how do we capture the kernel-level timing? we don't have access to the infra metrics on your cluster.
[06:05] Samir: we'll provide an annotated trace that includes the serving runtime events we can expose: batch assembly time, kernel exec time, kv cache lookup time, network serialization, etc. it's not raw perf counters but it gives enough to attribute where p99 heat comes from.
[06:20] Priya: okay. regarding network: is peering strictly necessary? can we do AWS PrivateLink?
[06:27] Alex: PrivateLink is possible but some customers prefer VPC peering or Direct Connect for lower network hops. PrivateLink reduces public egress but still goes through the provider's endpoints. peering (or Direct Connect) tends to have lower RTT and fewer NAT hops — fewer tail surprises.
[06:44] Susan: we have a Direct Connect path to our colo but we'd need paperwork.
[06:50] Alex: understood. we can note that in the topology doc.
[06:54] [06:54] Tom: another question — are there recommended batching parameters for models ~7B? we tried batch size 8 with continuous batching and saw higher throughput but some p99 regressions under burst.
[07:07] Samir: batch size is workload dependent. continuous batching reduces user-visible batching windows by greedily assembling requests, but if you have uneven request sizes, a single large request can block the batch. micro-batching (bounded batch with max-wait) is common: max-batch-size 8, max-wait 15ms. also make sure you have request shaping upstream to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[07:29] Priya: head-of-line — so if a big request sits in the batch it delays small ones?
[07:33] Jordan: yes. that's why we recommend size-based bucketing: small/short vs large requests go to different batch queues. that reduces tail for short interactive calls.
[07:44] Tom: can Redwood's runtime do per-route batching? for us different endpoints have different SLAs.
[07:50] Samir: yes, you can configure per-route batching windows and max batch size. and you can pin high-priority routes to a smaller pool to keep them isolated — that's a Dedicated config usually.
[08:02] Priya: is there any instrumentation we should add on our side to correlate app-level time to the runtime events?
[08:09] Jordan: put a unique request-id per call and log timestamps at ingress, pre-call to Redwood, and post-call. then our profiler's logs (which include the request-id) let you join the traces. also include a small payload hash to validate matching.
[08:23] [08:23] Tom: we'll add that.
[08:26] Alex: circling back — let's prioritize these experiments: (1) run the profiler with current streaming config, (2) run micro-batching scenario with size bucketing, (3) run quantized model (q4_0) to compare. Samir will supply the scripts.
[08:40] Samir: I'll also add a small test that simulates Transit Gateway latency by adding representative RTT in our harness to see sensitivity.
[08:48] Priya: good. one last question — any known interaction between TLS termination and tail? our egress terminates TLS at the NAT/proxy.
[08:57] Jordan: TLS can add a few ms and CPU spikes can cause jitter. persistent tls sessions and keepalives help. also, avoid small fragmented packets — serialization size matters.
[09:10] Susan: noted.
[09:15] Alex: ok, let's wrap up. quick recap in case the recorder is fuzzy.
[09:20] Alex: recap: you have p95/p99 goals 100/250 ms, current tails at ~420ms. probable contributors: KV cache eviction storms, multi-hop VPC egress via Transit Gateway/NAT, and batching/window config. Next steps: Samir shares profiler and annotated runtime trace; Priya shares staging VPC diagram and egress details; Tom runs three baselines (streaming, micro-batch, quantized). Alex sends pricing and topology note. We'll meet back after results.
[09:48] Priya: that timeline works; we'll aim to have initial artifacts by next week.
[09:55] Tom: thanks everyone.
[09:58] Alex: thanks, end call.
